ety.text: Biblical Hebrew אָמֵןbor. Koine Greek ᾱ̓μήν (āmḗn)bor. Ecclesiastical Latin āmēnder. Old English āmen Middle English amen English amen Inherited from Middle English amen, from Old English āmen, from Ecclesiastical Latin āmēn, from Ancient Greek ἀμήν (amḗn), from Biblical Hebrew אָמֵן (ʾāmēn, “certainly, verily”) (cognate with Arabic آمِينَ (ʔāmīna), Classical Syriac ܐܡܝܢ (ʾāmên)). In Old English, it was used only at the end of the Gospels; elsewhere, it was translated as sōþlīċe! (“truly, indeed!”), swā hit is (“so it is”), and sīe! (“[so] be it!”).

senses.d: At the end of a religious prayer: so be it.
ex: As it was in the beginning, is nowe, and euerſhall be: worlde without ende. Amen.
For thine is the kingdom, the power, and the glory, for ever and ever. Amen.

senses.d: Used to indicate emphatic agreement.
ex: Fry: Bender's stupid religion is driving me nuts! / Leela: Amen!

senses.d: Certainly; verily.
ex: Iesvs anſvvered, Amen, Amen I ſay to thee, Vnles a man be borne againe of vvater and the Spirit, he can not enter into the kingdom of God.

senses.d: An instance of saying ‘amen’.
ex: The amens of the dusty clerk appear, like Macbeth’s, to stick in his throat a little; but Captain Cuttle helps him out, […]
[H]is `Amens' were ejected at the pulpit with the severity of a reprimand.

senses.d: To say amen.
ex: The moment Dr. Reid amened, we rushed straight out of the church off home.
Most of the church amened and applauded.

senses.d: To say amen to; to ratify solemnly.
ex: spending the first half of the rally amening any mention of God or Reagan

ex: The First Amendment guarantees freedom of religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition.
The Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution abolished slavery.

senses.d: That which is added; that which is used to increase or supplement something.

ety.text: From Middle English amenden, from Old French amender, from Latin ēmendō (“free from faults”), from ex (“from, out of”) + mendum (“fault”). Compare aphetic mend. Doublet of emend.

senses.d: To make better; improve.
ex:
Mud not the fountain that gave drink to thee;
Mar not the thing that cannot be amended.
We shall cheer her sorrows, and amend her blood, by wedding her to a Norman.

senses.d: To become better.
To heal (someone sick); to cure (a disease etc.).
ex: he gave her a vomit, and conveyed a serpent, such as she conceived, into the basin; upon the sight of it she was amended.

senses.d: To be healed, to be cured, to recover (from an illness).
To make a formal alteration (in legislation, a report, etc.) by adding, deleting, or rephrasing.
ex: We amended the rules so that we could admit 20 more members to the club.

senses.d: An act of righting a wrong; compensation.
ex: Did I owe him an amend? Probably not, but I did owe myself an amend. I did this by ceasing to resent.
